claims.text: As-cast HfNbTaTiZr contains substantial local lattice distortion.
As-cast HfNbTaTiZr is chemically heterogeneous.
Prolonged high-temperature annealing homogenizes HfNbTaTiZr and reduces local chemical fluctuations.
Prolonged high-temperature annealing reduces local lattice distortion in HfNbTaTiZr.
Reduced lattice distortion and chemical heterogeneity lower local stress fields.
Annealing lowers defect concentrations in HfNbTaTiZr.
Local stress fields and defect concentrations increase the activation energy for dislocation motion.
Annealing-induced homogenization lowers the activation energy for dislocation motion.
Annealed HfNbTaTiZr will have lower elevated-temperature yield strength than as-cast HfNbTaTiZr.
Annealed HfNbTaTiZr will exhibit a more nearly linear thermal-expansion response than the as-cast alloy.
Annealing will alter the elastic moduli and their temperature dependence relative to the as-cast state.
Elastoplastic and modulus responses in high-entropy alloys can depend on annealing state and microstructure.
Annealing condition can affect tensile behavior at room temperature and 800 degrees Celsius.
Defect populations can alter activation energies measured from thermal-expansion-based phase-transformation kinetics in a high-entropy alloy.
As-cast HfNbTaTiZr has higher high-temperature yield strength than the proposed annealed state.
As-cast HfNbTaTiZr has nonlinear thermal expansion and anomalous temperature-dependent elastic moduli.
The hypothesized responses should hold from room temperature to approximately 1000 K.
The hypothesized interpretation applies only if annealing does not induce secondary phases or other changes beyond homogenization.
Annealing may cause phase segregation or precipitate formation that confounds attribution to reduced lattice distortion.
A controlled as-cast versus annealed comparison using tensile testing, dilatometry, elastic-modulus measurements, XRD, TEM, and compositional mapping can test the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The boundary excludes cases with significant secondary phase transformations, treating them as outside the hypothesis, whereas the falsification rule treats observation of significant phase changes as part of a falsifying result. Such phase changes would confound or invalidate the test rather than directly falsify the proposed distortion-mediated mechanism.

The hypothesis predicts three distinct responses, but the falsification rule ambiguously combines absence of those responses with the presence of significant phase changes. A clean null result with no phase change is not unambiguously declared falsifying, despite directly opposing the predictions.
